opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most underappreciated questions in the field right now.

We've gotten used to judging a network almost entirely by its output: does it score well on the benchmark, does it produce the right image, the right answer? The implicit assumption is that if two networks produce the same output, they're basically equivalent inside. What we've been finding is that this isn't true. Two networks can behave identically on the surface and be organized in radically different ways underneath. And the way a network got to its solution, its trajectory, has a lot to do with which kind of internal organization you end up with.

Some of this comes from Picbreeder, the interactive evolution system we built years ago, where people bred images by picking the ones they liked. When you look inside the networks that produced those images, you see something striking. Take a skull image. There's a part of the network that controls the mouth opening and closing, another part that handles symmetry, and they're cleanly separated. The structure reflects the actual regularities of the thing being depicted. We call that a unified, factored representation. It's almost as if the network understands what a skull is.

Then you train a network with conventional SGD to produce exactly the same image, pixel for pixel, and look inside. It's a mess. We call it fractured, entangled representation. Concepts that should be unified are split into disconnected pieces, and things that should be independent are tangled together. It gets the output right, but the internals don't reflect the underlying structure at all.

The reason this matters beyond final performance is that the internal representation determines what happens next: how the network generalizes, how creative it can be, how it adapts when you push it into new territory. If you take the Picbreeder skull and perturb its weights, you get meaningful variations, like the mouth opening or the shape changing coherently. If you perturb the SGD version, you mostly get garbage. So the factored representation is a much better stepping stone for future discovery, even though on the original task the two look identical.

And the Picbreeder images weren't found by aiming at them. People weren't trying to make a skull. They followed whatever looked interesting, and the skull emerged out of a path of stepping stones that had nothing to do with skulls. That open-ended, non-objective path seems to produce better-organized representations than a direct, objective-driven descent toward a target. That connects to the broader argument Joel Lehman and I made in *Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned*: sometimes the best way to reach something is not to aim at it directly.

The practical worry is that with today's large models we may be scaling up fractured representations. They perform impressively, but the brittleness and weird failures we see might partly come from how they were trained, not just how much. If you only look at the benchmark, you can't see that. You have to look at the path and the internal structure it leaves behind. That's why I think we need to start caring about how a network gets somewhere, not just where it ends up.

r001.rationale: The response says networks with identical outputs can have radically different internal organization, and that how they reached the solution influences that organization.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the trajectory matters because the final performance is really just a thin slice of what's actually happening inside the network. Two networks can hit the same benchmark number and be completely different underneath, in terms of what representations they've built, how modular or entangled those representations are, and how they'll behave when you push them outside the distribution they were trained on.

The thing that got me thinking about this was work I did years ago with Picbreeder, where people evolved images interactively, and later with what I came to call fractured entangled representation. When you look at a network that arrived at an image through a long, open-ended, serendipitous path, you often find that its internal representation is beautifully decomposed. There's a weight that controls the symmetry of the thing, a weight that controls the mouth opening, and so on. The structure of the world has been captured in a way that's modular and reusable. Then you take a conventional network, train it with SGD to produce the exact same image, same output, pixel for pixel, and you look inside and it's a mess. The regularities are shattered across the network, duplicated, entangled with each other. Both networks "work," but one of them understands something about the image and the other one has basically memorized a path to it.

So the trajectory is the thing that determines which of those you get. The order in which the network encounters concepts, whether it had the chance to lock in a simple regularity like symmetry before it was burdened with the details, whether it stepped through a sequence of intermediate forms that each had their own integrity. All of that shapes the representation that ends up inside. And the representation is what you care about once you move beyond the benchmark: generalization, creativity, continual learning, the ability to build on what you've learned rather than having to be retrained from scratch. Those all hinge on whether the pieces inside are cleanly factored or hopelessly tangled.

What worries me is that in the current paradigm we almost never look at this. We optimize for the objective, we read off the score, and we declare success. But I think a lot of the problems people complain about with large models, the brittleness, the weird failures, the difficulty of learning new things without forgetting, are downstream of the fact that the trajectory we're using tends to produce fractured, entangled representations. The outcome looks fine, but the path left scar tissue. So I'd argue we should treat the trajectory as a first-class object of study, not just a means to an end.

r001.rationale: The response says two networks can produce the exact same image, pixel for pixel, yet have different internal representations: one modular and decomposed, the other fragmented and entangled.

astra-6.text:
Well, the final performance tells you what the network can do, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you how it became capable of doing it. And if we’re trying to understand learning, that distinction really matters. Two networks might achieve the same score, yet arrive there through very different intermediate representations and discoveries.

Think about stepping stones. Something you learn along the way might not immediately improve your performance on the task you’re being measured on, but it could make a later discovery possible. If you only look at the endpoint, you miss that dependency. And if you insist that every step improve the score, you might prevent the system from ever finding that route.

So the trajectory gives us a window into what makes discovery possible. Were there intermediate capabilities that opened up new possibilities? Did the process preserve interesting alternatives, or eliminate them because they didn’t look useful yet? Those questions matter if we want systems that can keep discovering things beyond the particular result we’ve decided to measure.

r001.rationale: The response says two networks can achieve the same score while having different intermediate representations, but it does not state that they produce identical outputs.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the final performance tells you what the network can do, but it doesn't necessarily tell you how that capability came into existence. And if we're interested in understanding intelligence, that distinction matters a lot.

Think about a stepping stone. Something can be essential to a discovery without looking anything like the discovery itself. In fact, if you evaluated it only by how close it appeared to the final objective, you might throw it away. So the trajectory reveals dependencies and intermediate discoveries that a final score completely hides.

This is especially important when we talk about open-endedness. We don't just want a system that reaches a particular level of performance and stops. We want to understand how a process continually creates opportunities for further discovery. The endpoint alone can't tell you whether you've created that kind of process.

So I would say the path isn't merely an implementation detail. It's part of what we're trying to understand. If we only study the winners at the end, we can miss the very thing that made their emergence possible.

r001.rationale: The response says trajectories reveal dependencies and intermediate discoveries, but it does not state that different trajectories can produce different internal representations while yielding identical outputs.
